question_text: A 35-year-old male sustained full-thickness burns to 20% of his total body surface area (TBSA) involving the right anterior arm and hand. He is 3 weeks post-injury. Which physiotherapy intervention is MOST critical to prevent a long-term functional deficit in this patient?
option_a: Aggressive passive stretching of all joints under general anaesthesia
option_b: Burn scar management including pressure garments, silicone, and active and active-assisted ROM exercises to maintain joint mobility and prevent hypertrophic scarring and contracture
option_c: Complete immobilization of the hand to allow graft healing
option_d: Hydrotherapy wound cleansing three times daily as the sole intervention
rationale: Full-thickness burns and skin grafting are major risk factors for hypertrophic scar formation and joint contracture, particularly in the hand and elbow (critical for function). Early mobilization (active and active-assisted ROM), positioning, splinting, and pressure garments combined with silicone gel sheets are the cornerstones of burn rehabilitation to prevent contracture and functional loss. Immobilization causes contracture. Pressure therapy should begin as soon as wounds are 90% healed (typically 3 weeks).

question_text: A 55-year-old female who is 8 months post-right mastectomy is referred for physiotherapy with a diagnosis of right breast cancer-related lymphedema (Stage II). She presents with right arm pitting edema, heaviness, and skin changes. Which component is MOST essential in the Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT) protocol?
option_a: High-voltage electrical stimulation over the edematous limb
option_b: Manual lymphatic drainage (MLD), multi-layer lymphedema bandaging, exercise, and skin care as integrated components of CDT
option_c: Diuretic medication as the primary intervention
option_d: Pneumatic compression pump as the sole intervention
rationale: Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT) is the gold standard for lymphedema management. Phase I (intensive) includes: Manual Lymphatic Drainage (stimulates lymphatic rerouting), multilayer inelastic bandaging (provides containment and pressure gradient), therapeutic exercise (promotes lymph flow via muscle pump), and meticulous skin care (prevent infection/cellulitis). All components are integrated and essential. CDT Phase II (maintenance) transitions to compression garments. No single component alone is equivalent to the full CDT protocol.

question_text: A 62-year-old male with Parkinson's disease is referred to physiotherapy for speech difficulties. The physiotherapist notes he has hypophonia (reduced voice volume) and monopitch. Which referral and approach is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Begin phonation exercises independently as physiotherapists are trained to treat all aspects of Parkinson's disease
option_b: Refer to a speech-language pathologist (SLP) for assessment and treatment of hypophonia, while the physiotherapist addresses associated respiratory support through breathing exercises as part of interdisciplinary management
option_c: Prescribe deep breathing exercises only as the sole management of hypophonia
option_d: Defer all communication concerns to the neurologist
rationale: Hypophonia and monopitch in Parkinson's disease are communication disorders within the scope of speech-language pathology. The LSVT-LOUD program (Lee Silverman Voice Treatment) is the gold-standard SLP intervention. The physiotherapist should refer to SLP while recognizing their own role in supporting respiratory muscle function (relevant to voice support) as part of interprofessional care. This demonstrates appropriate scope of practice boundaries and collaborative care.

question_text: A physiotherapist is working in a school setting with an 8-year-old child with developmental coordination disorder (DCD). The child struggles with ball-catching, handwriting, and balance tasks. Which approach has the STRONGEST evidence base for improving motor skills in DCD?
option_a: Deficit-specific bottom-up remediation of identified motor component deficits (e.g., isolated balance board training)
option_b: Task-oriented (top-down) intervention focusing on practicing specific functional tasks the child finds difficult, within meaningful contexts, using principles of motor learning
option_c: Sensory integration therapy using suspended equipment and deep pressure
option_d: Complete avoidance of challenging motor tasks to prevent frustration and reduced self-efficacy
rationale: Task-oriented (top-down) approaches — particularly the Neuromotor Task Training (NTT) and CO-OP (Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance) frameworks — have the strongest evidence for DCD. These approaches focus on practicing specific functional tasks that are meaningful to the child, using motor learning principles (variable practice, feedback, problem-solving). Bottom-up sensorimotor approaches and sensory integration therapy have weaker evidence for DCD functional outcomes.

question_text: A 48-year-old female is 6 weeks post-partum and reports leakage of urine when coughing, sneezing, and jumping. She had a vaginal delivery with a 2nd degree perineal tear. Pelvic floor muscle strength assessment reveals grade 3/5 bilaterally. What is the FIRST-LINE physiotherapy intervention?
option_a: Refer for surgical sling procedure
option_b: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program: progressive graded Kegel exercises with correct technique, beginning with low-load holds and progressing to higher-load functional activities
option_c: Prescribe a pessary device without any exercise
option_d: Recommend avoidance of all physical activity for 6 months
rationale: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is the evidence-based first-line physiotherapy intervention for post-partum stress urinary incontinence. Grade 3/5 pelvic floor strength indicates functional muscle contraction against gravity — the patient can benefit from graded progressive resistance training. PFMT programs typically include progressive hold durations (building from 3–10 second holds) and functional integration (contracting before coughing/sneezing — the "knack" technique). Surgery is considered only after conservative physiotherapy fails.

question_text: A physiotherapist sees a patient referred by an orthopedic surgeon with a diagnosis of "right knee pain — treat." On assessment, the physiotherapist identifies findings suggestive of deep vein thrombosis (positive Wells score, calf pain and swelling). Which action BEST demonstrates the physiotherapist's professional responsibility?
option_a: Treat the knee pain as directed by the referring physician and document the calf findings
option_b: Immediately refer the patient back to the physician or emergency services for DVT investigation, clearly communicating the clinical findings and concerns
option_c: Apply a compression bandage to the calf and reassess in 48 hours
option_d: Defer to the physician's referral and treat the knee as prescribed
rationale: Physiotherapists are regulated autonomous health professionals responsible for their own clinical assessments and decisions. When a physiotherapist identifies clinical signs suggesting a potentially life-threatening condition (DVT with risk of pulmonary embolism), the professional and ethical duty is to act on those findings — including referring urgently to emergency services or the physician — regardless of the referral diagnosis. Acting solely on a physician's referral without exercising independent clinical judgment falls below the standard of practice.

question_text: A physiotherapy clinic wants to implement an outcome measurement program. They plan to measure patient-reported outcomes at intake, mid-treatment, and discharge. Which property of an outcome measure is MOST important to ensure the measure can detect genuine change over time?
option_a: Face validity — that the measure looks like it measures what it is supposed to measure
option_b: Responsiveness (sensitivity to change) — that the measure can detect clinically meaningful change when true change occurs
option_c: Test-retest reliability alone
option_d: Inter-rater reliability
rationale: Responsiveness (also called sensitivity to change) is the psychometric property that determines whether an outcome measure can detect real changes over time when they occur. For longitudinal outcome monitoring programs (intake to discharge), an unresponsive measure would fail to reflect genuine patient improvement or deterioration, rendering the data clinically useless. While reliability and validity are necessary prerequisites, responsiveness is the most critical property for detecting treatment effects in clinical practice.

question_text: A physiotherapist in a private clinic has a personal injury claim patient (MVA) whose insurer calls directly to inquire about the patient's progress and expected return-to-work date. The physiotherapist should:
option_a: Provide the insurer with full details of the assessment and treatment to facilitate the claim
option_b: Decline to share patient health information without the patient's explicit written consent, and direct the insurer to obtain a formal written authorization from the patient
option_c: Provide a brief verbal summary only to keep the communication efficient
option_d: Share information freely as insurers have implied access to patient health records for claims purposes
rationale: Patient health information is confidential and cannot be shared with any third party — including insurers — without the patient's explicit written consent, regardless of who is funding the treatment. Canadian privacy legislation (PIPEDA, provincial health privacy acts) and physiotherapy professional standards require written patient authorization before disclosure to insurers. The insurer must obtain a signed release of information form from the patient before the physiotherapist can share clinical details.

question_text: A 40-year-old male tennis player presents with right shoulder pain during the late cocking and acceleration phases of serving. On examination, there is posterior shoulder tightness (internal rotation deficit of 25° compared to left), and positive impingement signs. His external rotation strength is 4/5. Which condition is MOST consistent with this presentation in an overhead athlete?
option_a: Acromioclavicular joint sprain
option_b: Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) with secondary subacromial impingement
option_c: Biceps tendon rupture
option_d: Subscapularis tear
rationale: Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit (GIRD) is a common finding in overhead athletes caused by posterior capsule and rotator cuff tightness. Loss of internal rotation (≥20° difference) shifts the glenohumeral contact point posterosuperiorly, increasing impingement risk and predisposing to labral pathology. The pain pattern during the cocking and acceleration phases of overhead throwing/serving is characteristic. Treatment includes posterior capsule stretching (sleeper stretch), rotator cuff strengthening, and scapular stabilization.

question_text: A 48-year-old female presents with right wrist and hand pain and numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers that is worse at night and with sustained gripping. The Phalen's test is positive at 30 seconds and Tinel's sign is positive over the carpal tunnel. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
option_a: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
option_b: Carpal tunnel syndrome
option_c: Ulnar nerve entrapment at Guyon's canal
option_d: C6 cervical radiculopathy
rationale: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) classically presents with numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial ring fingers), nocturnal symptoms, positive Phalen's test (sustained wrist flexion reproduces symptoms in <60 seconds), and positive Tinel's sign over the carpal tunnel. De Quervain's affects the radial aspect of the wrist at the first dorsal compartment. Guyon's canal affects the ulnar digits (ring and small finger). C6 radiculopathy would include neck and arm symptoms.

question_text: During gait analysis, a physiotherapist observes that a 55-year-old male with right knee OA exhibits excessive lateral trunk lean over the right stance limb. What is the MOST likely biomechanical explanation for this compensation?
option_a: He is reducing hip abductor demand by shifting his center of mass over the stance limb, thereby reducing the knee adduction moment at the right knee
option_b: He is increasing the hip abductor demand to stabilize the pelvis during stance
option_c: He is compensating for right Achilles tendon tightness
option_d: This is a reflexive pattern to avoid right knee flexion during stance
rationale: In knee OA, the knee adduction moment is a key driver of medial compartment loading and pain. Lateral trunk lean (Duchenne gait) over the stance limb shifts the body's center of mass laterally toward the knee, reducing the moment arm of the ground reaction force from the joint and thereby reducing the knee adduction moment and medial compartment load. It also reduces the demand on hip abductors (reducing hip abductor force which otherwise increases compressive joint load). This is a pain-reducing compensation, though it loads the hip and lumbar spine.

question_text: A 19-year-old female cross-country runner is referred to physiotherapy with a 3-week history of right anterior shin pain that begins after approximately 10 minutes of running and resolves with rest. The compartment feels tight during symptoms. Passive stretch of the right ankle into dorsiflexion reproduces her symptoms during running. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints)
option_b: Exercise-induced (chronic exertional) compartment syndrome of the right anterior compartment
option_c: Tibial stress fracture
option_d: Common peroneal nerve entrapment
rationale: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS) presents with predictable onset of pain and tightness during exercise (onset at a reproducible time/distance), compartment tightness during symptoms, and rapid relief with cessation of activity. It predominantly affects the anterior compartment in runners. Passive dorsiflexion stretch during symptomatic episodes increases intra-compartmental pressure and reproduces symptoms. Medial tibial stress syndrome is bony/periosteal pain along the posteromedial tibia. Stress fracture has focal bony tenderness on palpation.

question_text: A 66-year-old male with COPD is being assessed using spirometry results. His FEV1 is 38% predicted and his FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.55. Based on the GOLD classification system, what GOLD stage does this represent?
option_a: GOLD Stage I (Mild)
option_b: GOLD Stage II (Moderate)
option_c: GOLD Stage III (Severe)
option_d: GOLD Stage IV (Very Severe)
rationale: The GOLD classification stages COPD severity based on post-bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted (with confirmed obstruction: FEV1/FVC <0.70): Stage I ≥80%, Stage II 50–79%, Stage III 30–49%, Stage IV <30%. An FEV1 of 38% predicted falls within the Stage III (Severe) range. The FEV1/FVC of 0.55 (<0.70) confirms airflow obstruction. This patient meets criteria for GOLD Stage III COPD.

question_text: A 60-year-old male with a history of heavy smoking and chronic sun exposure presents with a non-healing ulcer on his lower lip that has been present for 8 weeks. It has raised, indurated borders and the patient reports painlessness. What is the MOST important action for the physiotherapist?
option_a: Apply a moist wound dressing and review in 4 weeks
option_b: Recognize this as a potential malignant lesion (possible squamous cell carcinoma) and refer urgently to a physician or dermatologist for biopsy
option_c: Begin laser therapy to the lesion
option_d: Prescribe oral antifungal treatment
rationale: A non-healing wound (>6 weeks) with raised, indurated, rolled borders in a patient with significant cancer risk factors (heavy smoking, chronic sun exposure) on the lip is a red flag for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Oral SCC can be rapidly progressive. The physiotherapist must recognize this as outside the scope of wound care and refer urgently for medical assessment and biopsy. Treating a potentially malignant lesion as a routine wound delays critical diagnosis.

question_text: A 70-year-old male with osteoporosis (DEXA T-score -2.9 at the lumbar spine) is referred to physiotherapy. Which exercise type is MOST contraindicated for this patient?
option_a: Walking program on level ground
option_b: Spinal flexion exercises (e.g., abdominal crunches, toe-touch stretches) which increase vertebral body compression forces and fracture risk
option_c: Progressive resistance training using machines
option_d: Hip extension strengthening exercises
rationale: In osteoporosis, particularly with vertebral involvement (lumbar T-score -2.9), spinal flexion exercises significantly increase anterior vertebral body compressive loading and are associated with increased vertebral fracture risk. Exercises such as sit-ups, forward bending toe-touches, and rowing movements are contraindicated. Evidence-based osteoporosis exercise programs (e.g., the FLEX program, BEST trials) emphasize spinal extension, weight-bearing aerobic activity, and progressive resistance training while avoiding flexion-dominant spinal loading.

question_text: A physiotherapist is reading a research paper that reports a sensitivity of 85% and specificity of 70% for a clinical test used to diagnose ACL tears. A patient presents with a pre-test probability of ACL tear of 60% (based on mechanism and history). How should the physiotherapist use this information?
option_a: A positive test result definitively confirms ACL rupture and no further investigation is needed
option_b: Understanding sensitivity, specificity, and pre-test probability allows the physiotherapist to estimate post-test probability using likelihood ratios, informing clinical decision-making but not replacing diagnostic imaging
option_c: A sensitivity of 85% means the test will correctly identify 85% of all patients, regardless of prior probability
option_d: Specificity of 70% means the test will produce false positives in 70% of truly negative cases
rationale: Diagnostic reasoning integrates pre-test probability (based on clinical context), sensitivity, and specificity through likelihood ratios (LR+ = sensitivity / (1 – specificity) = 0.85/0.30 = 2.83; LR– = (1 – sensitivity) / specificity = 0.15/0.70 = 0.21). With a 60% pre-test probability, a positive test raises post-test probability to approximately 81% (using Bayes' theorem / Fagan's nomogram). A positive result supports but does not definitively confirm ACL rupture — MRI remains the diagnostic gold standard. Clinical tests inform probability estimates, not definitive diagnoses.

question_text: For the patient with Parkinson's disease experiencing freezing of gait (FOG) at doorways, which cueing strategy has the MOST evidence for immediate gait initiation at this specific location?
option_a: Verbal counting cadence delivered by a caregiver
option_b: Rhythmic auditory stimulation using a portable metronome
option_c: Transverse visual floor line cues placed at the threshold
option_d: Mental imagery of stepping over an obstacle
rationale: Visual transverse line cues (floor markings) placed at threshold transitions such as doorways are the most evidence-supported external cue for FOG in Parkinson's disease. They provide a salient attentional trigger that bypasses defective automaticity by engaging the visual-motor system. Auditory and verbal cues are also used but visual floor cues are especially effective at specific locations like doorways.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 71-year-old male with a 9-year history of Parkinson's disease (Hoehn & Yahr Stage 3) is referred to physiotherapy. He reports frequent freezing of gait (FOG) when approaching doorways and turning, and has fallen twice in the past month. Examination: shuffling gait, reduced arm swing bilaterally, hypophonia, resting tremor right hand. UPDRS motor score: 38. He lives at home with his wife and is on levodopa/carbidopa. He is interested in joining an LSVT BIG program.

question_text: The patient's wife asks about the LSVT BIG program structure. Which of the following BEST describes the standard delivery format?
option_a: Once weekly for 12 weeks with daily home exercise
option_b: Three times per week for 6 weeks with biweekly monitoring
option_c: Daily sessions for 2 weeks followed by monthly maintenance
option_d: Four times per week for 4 consecutive weeks, one hour per session
rationale: LSVT BIG follows a standardized protocol of 4 individual sessions per week for 4 consecutive weeks (16 sessions total), each lasting approximately 1 hour. This high-intensity, high-amplitude training model is based on the same principles as LSVT LOUD and has Level 1 evidence for improving motor function in Parkinson's disease.

question_text: Given that this patient is Hoehn & Yahr Stage 3 and has fallen twice in the past month, which fall prevention intervention should be the HIGHEST priority in his physiotherapy plan?
option_a: Ankle strengthening exercises in seated position
option_b: Dual-task balance training under variable environmental conditions
option_c: Recumbent cycling for cardiovascular conditioning
option_d: Passive stretching of bilateral hip flexors
rationale: H&Y Stage 3 indicates bilateral disease with postural instability but maintained independence. Dual-task balance training addresses the primary mechanism of falls in Parkinson's — impaired automaticity leading to failure under cognitive load. This directly targets the attentional demands of real-world walking and is prioritized over isolated strengthening or flexibility work.

question_text: Using the Wagner Ulcer Classification System, how should this patient's plantar ulcer be classified?
option_a: Wagner Grade 1 — superficial ulcer involving dermis only
option_b: Wagner Grade 2 — deep ulcer penetrating to subcutaneous tissue without bone involvement
option_c: Wagner Grade 3 — deep ulcer with osteitis or abscess
option_d: Wagner Grade 4 — partial foot gangrene
rationale: Wagner Grade 2 describes a deep full-thickness ulcer penetrating to subcutaneous tissue, tendon, ligament, or joint capsule but without bone involvement. This patient's 0.5 cm deep wound with visible subcutaneous tissue and no palpable bone fits Grade 2. Grade 1 involves only the dermis; Grade 3 requires osteitis or deep infection.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 58-year-old male with a 20-year history of Type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 9.2%) presents to a wound care clinic. He has a 3 cm × 2.5 cm plantar ulcer at the first metatarsal head of his right foot, depth 0.5 cm, with visible subcutaneous tissue. No bone is palpable. The wound bed has 60% granulation tissue and 40% slough. Periwound skin is callused. Protective sensation is absent bilaterally using 10g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament. ABI right foot: 0.82.

question_text: Which offloading device is considered the GOLD STANDARD for plantar diabetic foot ulcers located at the first metatarsal head?
option_a: Removable cast walker (RCW) with felt padding
option_b: Custom-molded orthotics in extra-depth footwear
option_c: Total contact cast (TCC)
option_d: Accommodative foam dressing with heel wedge
rationale: Total contact cast (TCC) is the gold standard for plantar diabetic neuropathic ulcers. It distributes pressure across the entire plantar surface, is non-removable (ensuring compliance), and has the highest evidence for ulcer healing. Removable cast walkers are second-line because patients often remove them, reducing offloading time to under 30% of ambulatory hours.

question_text: This patient's ABI is 0.82. What is the MOST appropriate clinical interpretation regarding wound management options?
option_a: Critical limb ischaemia; immediate vascular surgery referral is required before any wound care
option_b: Normal perfusion; proceed with standard high-compression bandaging at 40 mmHg
option_c: Severe arterial insufficiency; avoid offloading and use elevation only
option_d: Mild peripheral arterial disease; compression is generally safe with careful monitoring
rationale: ABI 0.81–0.90 indicates mild peripheral arterial disease. Compression therapy is not absolutely contraindicated but should be used cautiously with reduced pressures and careful monitoring. ABI <0.5 indicates critical ischaemia requiring urgent vascular referral. ABI >0.9 is considered normal. This neuropathic ulcer primarily requires offloading, and the ABI guides judgment about any additional compression component.

question_text: For this patient on Day 2 following 3-vessel CABG, which activity BEST represents appropriate Phase 1 cardiac rehabilitation?
option_a: Dangling at the bedside followed by standing and corridor ambulation of approximately 50 feet
option_b: Stationary cycling at 50 W for 20 minutes
option_c: Upper extremity ergometer at 30 W for 10 minutes
option_d: Stair climbing practice to prepare for discharge home
rationale: Phase 1 inpatient cardiac rehabilitation on Day 2 post-CABG focuses on progressive mobilization beginning with sitting on the edge of the bed (dangling), progressing to standing, then short corridor ambulation with vital sign monitoring. Goals are prevention of deconditioning, atelectasis, and DVT. High-intensity exercise and UE ergometry are contraindicated with an acute sternotomy.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 61-year-old male is on Day 2 following a 3-vessel coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) via median sternotomy. He is in the cardiac surgery ICU. Vitals: HR 78 bpm, BP 118/72, SpO2 96% on 2L nasal cannula. He has a midline sternotomy incision with staples, bilateral chest tubes (draining minimal output), and a Foley catheter. He has not been out of bed since surgery.

question_text: Regarding sternal precautions post-median sternotomy, which movement restriction is MOST critical in the acute phase to protect sternal stability?
option_a: Avoiding cervical rotation beyond 45 degrees bilaterally
option_b: Avoiding bilateral simultaneous upper extremity pushing and pulling activities
option_c: Restricting knee flexion beyond 90 degrees during transfers
option_d: Avoiding shoulder abduction past 90 degrees on the dominant side only
rationale: Sternal precautions focus on protecting the healing sternotomy. The most critical restriction is avoiding bilateral simultaneous upper extremity pushing, pulling, and lifting, which creates shear and distraction forces across the sternotomy. Bilateral UE activities symmetrically load the sternum and risk sternal dehiscence. Asymmetric, light UE movements during daily tasks may be permitted under some institutional protocols.

question_text: What is the PRIMARY physiological purpose of prescribing incentive spirometry to this post-CABG patient in the ICU?
option_a: To strengthen the diaphragm weakened by general anaesthesia
option_b: To deliver aerosolized bronchodilator medication to distal airways
option_c: To prevent and treat postoperative atelectasis by promoting sustained maximal inspiration
option_d: To measure forced expiratory volume as a marker of daily recovery
rationale: Incentive spirometry provides visual biofeedback to encourage slow, deep, sustained maximal inspirations (SMI). After cardiac surgery via sternotomy, reduced tidal volumes due to pain, splinting, and recumbency predispose to alveolar collapse (atelectasis). Sustained maximal inspiration reopens collapsed alveoli via collateral ventilation channels. It does not measure FEV1 nor deliver medication.

question_text: Based on the clinical findings (C6 dermatomal sensory loss, reduced biceps reflex, grip weakness, positive Spurling's, positive right ULTTA), which nerve root is MOST likely involved?
option_a: C5 — lateral arm and deltoid distribution
option_b: C7 — middle finger and triceps reflex
option_c: C8 — ring and little finger distribution
option_d: C6 — thumb and index finger with biceps reflex involvement
rationale: C6 radiculopathy presents with: dermatomal distribution to the thumb and index finger, diminished biceps reflex (C5-6 reflex arc), weakness of wrist extensors and biceps, and reproduction with Spurling's and ULTTA (median nerve bias). C5 affects the lateral arm and deltoid. C7 affects the middle finger and triceps reflex. C8 affects the ring and little fingers.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 42-year-old office administrator presents with a 6-week history of right-sided neck pain radiating to the right thumb and index finger. She reports numbness and tingling in the same distribution and weakness when gripping. Neurological examination: reduced sensation C6 dermatomal distribution, biceps reflex 1+ (right) vs 2+ (left), grip strength 3/5 right vs 5/5 left. Spurling's test: positive reproducing right arm symptoms. Upper limb tension test A (ULTTA): positive right.

question_text: For this patient with confirmed C6 radiculopathy, which initial conservative physiotherapy intervention is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Cervical manipulation targeting C5-6 facet joints
option_b: Cervical mechanical traction combined with neural mobilization techniques
option_c: High-intensity cervical strengthening with isometric resistance loading
option_d: Dry needling to upper trapezius and levator scapulae trigger points
rationale: Cervical mechanical traction is a first-line evidence-based conservative intervention for cervical radiculopathy with neurological signs. It reduces foraminal pressure and discogenic compression. Neural mobilization (sliding and tensioning techniques) addresses neural mechanosensitivity. Cervical manipulation is relatively contraindicated with neurological deficits. High-intensity strengthening is inappropriate in the acute phase with active neurological compromise.

question_text: Which finding, if present during examination, would constitute a RED FLAG requiring IMMEDIATE referral for this patient with cervical radiculopathy?
option_a: Bilateral upper extremity paresthesia with gait disturbance and lower extremity hyperreflexia
option_b: Pain score 8/10 on NRS during Spurling's maneuver
option_c: Mild weakness (4/5) in wrist extension ipsilateral to the pain
option_d: Pain reproduced with sustained cervical extension past 30 degrees
rationale: Bilateral UE paresthesia combined with lower extremity hyperreflexia and gait disturbance is a clinical cluster indicating cervical myelopathy — cord compression — which is a surgical emergency requiring immediate referral. Unilateral pain, unilateral mild weakness, and pain on provocative testing are expected in radiculopathy and do not trigger immediate referral.

question_text: Based on the Dix-Hallpike findings (upbeat-torsional nystagmus geotropic toward the right ear, 3-second latency, 18-second duration, fatigable on repeat), what is the MOST likely diagnosis and affected structure?
option_a: Vestibular neuritis affecting the right vestibular nerve
option_b: Horizontal canal BPPV, geotropic variant, right side
option_c: Right posterior canal BPPV, canalithiasis — free-floating debris in the posterior semicircular canal
option_d: Right posterior canal BPPV, cupulolithiasis — debris adherent to the cupula
rationale: The classic triad of posterior canal BPPV canalithiasis: upbeat-torsional nystagmus toward the undermost ear (geotropic), onset latency 2–5 seconds (free-floating debris accelerating), duration <1 minute, and fatigability on repeated testing. Cupulolithiasis lacks latency and is non-fatigable. Vestibular neuritis causes persistent spontaneous nystagmus. Horizontal canal BPPV is tested with the roll test, not Dix-Hallpike.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 55-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of intense vertigo, nausea, and imbalance triggered by rolling over in bed to the right. Symptoms last approximately 30 seconds and then resolve. She denies hearing loss or tinnitus. Dix-Hallpike test: positive on the right with upbeat-torsional nystagmus geotropic toward the right ear, onset latency 3 seconds, duration 18 seconds, fatigable on repeat testing.

question_text: When performing the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver for this patient's right posterior canal BPPV, what is the CORRECT sequence of head positions?
option_a: Left lateral decubitus → supine neutral → right lateral decubitus → sit up
option_b: Semont liberatory: rapid turn from right Dix-Hallpike to left lateral position
option_c: Dix-Hallpike right → head rotated 45° left while supine → left lateral decubitus with nose down → sit up
option_d: Dix-Hallpike right → head rotated 90° left while supine → left lateral decubitus (nose-down) → sit up facing left
rationale: The Epley maneuver for right posterior BPPV: (1) Dix-Hallpike right to move debris to the apex of the posterior canal; (2) head rotated 90° to the left while remaining supine, allowing debris to move toward the common crus; (3) body rolled to left lateral decubitus (nose-down) moving debris toward the utricle; (4) patient sits up. Each position is held 30–60 seconds. Option C describes only 45° rotation which is insufficient.

question_text: Which nystagmus characteristic during positional testing would MOST strongly suggest a CENTRAL rather than peripheral cause of vertigo?
option_a: Upbeat-torsional nystagmus with 3-second latency that fatigues on repeat testing
option_b: Direction-changing nystagmus without latency that does not fatigue
option_c: Horizontal nystagmus elicited only in the right lateral decubitus position
option_d: Nystagmus that resolves within 30 seconds following position change
rationale: Central vertigo red flags include direction-changing nystagmus (changes direction with gaze), pure vertical or purely torsional nystagmus without latency, non-fatigable nystagmus, and inability to suppress with fixation. Direction-changing nystagmus without latency that does not fatigue strongly suggests a central lesion (cerebellar or brainstem) requiring urgent imaging. Peripheral BPPV nystagmus is latent, fatigable, and direction-fixed.

question_text: A 35-year-old recreational runner presents with lateral knee pain that worsens at the 30-minute mark of runs and is reproduced at 30° knee flexion during examination. The Noble compression test is positive. Which structure is MOST likely implicated?
option_a: Lateral collateral ligament
option_b: Iliotibial band at the lateral femoral epicondyle
option_c: Biceps femoris tendon at the fibular head
option_d: Lateral meniscus posterior horn
rationale: Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS) is the most common cause of lateral knee pain in runners. The Noble compression test applies pressure at the lateral femoral epicondyle at 30° of flexion, reproducing pain at the impingement zone where the ITB crosses the lateral femoral condyle. The '30-minute rule' and reproducibility at 30° flexion are hallmarks of ITBS.

question_text: A 52-year-old woman presents with insidious onset right shoulder pain worse at night. Passive ROM: flexion 110°, abduction 95°, external rotation 40°. Active ROM equals passive ROM. The empty can test is negative. Which diagnosis is MOST consistent?
option_a: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)
option_b: Subacromial bursitis with normal passive motion
option_c: Supraspinatus tendinopathy
option_d: Acromioclavicular joint sprain
rationale: Adhesive capsulitis is characterized by global passive ROM restriction following a capsular pattern (ER > abduction > flexion), with active equal to passive restriction indicating a non-contractile cause. The negative empty can test rules out significant rotator cuff pathology. Night pain and insidious onset in a middle-aged woman are classic features. Bursitis and tendinopathy would show full passive ROM.

question_text: During the assessment of a patient with acute low back pain, which finding would MOST indicate a serious pathology requiring urgent medical referral?
option_a: Bilateral sciatica with saddle anaesthesia and recent onset urinary retention
option_b: Positive SLR at 45° reproducing ipsilateral leg pain to the calf
option_c: Morning stiffness lasting 45 minutes with peripheral joint involvement
option_d: Pain that worsens with sustained lumbar flexion
rationale: Bilateral sciatica with saddle anaesthesia (perineal numbness) and urinary retention is a clinical presentation of cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency. Immediate referral is required to prevent permanent neurological deficit. All other options may indicate specific pathology but are not emergencies requiring immediate referral.

question_text: A physiotherapist performs McMurray's test on a patient with medial knee pain. A palpable click with pain on external tibial rotation moving from full flexion toward extension is MOST consistent with which finding?
option_a: Medial meniscus tear
option_b: Lateral meniscus tear (internal rotation test positive)
option_c: Medial collateral ligament sprain
option_d: Anterior cruciate ligament partial tear
rationale: McMurray's test: with the knee in full flexion, external rotation of the tibia with valgus stress tests the medial meniscus. A palpable/audible click or clunk with pain on the medial joint line during external rotation indicates a medial meniscus tear. Internal rotation tests the lateral meniscus. The test has high specificity for meniscal pathology when a true click is elicited.

question_text: A 60-year-old woman with osteoporosis reports acute thoracic back pain following sneezing. Imaging reveals a T8 vertebral compression fracture. Which physiotherapy intervention is CONTRAINDICATED?
option_a: Trunk flexion strengthening exercises (curl-ups and crunches)
option_b: Postural education for spinal neutral alignment
option_c: Progressive ambulation with an appropriate assistive device
option_d: Thoracic extension exercises over a foam roll
rationale: Trunk flexion exercises (crunches, sit-ups) significantly increase anterior vertebral body compressive forces, which can worsen or propagate osteoporotic compression fractures. Evidence from Sinaki et al. demonstrates that spinal flexion exercise increases fracture risk in patients with established vertebral fractures. Extension exercises are protective and are a cornerstone of osteoporotic fracture management.

question_text: A 45-year-old male presents with medial elbow pain, worsened by resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation. Which tendon is MOST likely involved?
option_a: Common flexor tendon (flexor carpi radialis) at the medial epicondyle
option_b: Triceps tendon at the olecranon
option_c: Common extensor tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle
option_d: Anconeus muscle at the lateral aspect of the elbow
rationale: Medial epicondylalgia (golfer's elbow) involves the common flexor tendon origin at the medial epicondyle, most commonly the flexor carpi radialis and pronator teres. Pain is reproduced by resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation. The common extensor tendon is implicated in lateral epicondylalgia. Triceps tendinopathy causes posterior elbow pain.

question_text: Which outcome measure is MOST appropriate to assess functional disability specifically in patients with knee osteoarthritis in a clinical research setting?
option_a: WOMAC (Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index)
option_b: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
option_c: Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS)
option_d: DASH (Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand)
rationale: The WOMAC is a validated disease-specific outcome measure for hip and knee osteoarthritis, assessing pain (5 items), stiffness (2 items), and physical function (17 items). It has excellent psychometric properties for OA populations. The LEFS is a general lower extremity tool; ODI is spine-specific; DASH is upper extremity-specific.

question_text: A 30-year-old female marathon runner presents with progressive medial tibial pain over 3 weeks. Focal point tenderness at a single site on the posteromedial tibial cortex, positive hop test, and night pain are present. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Tibial stress fracture
option_b: Deep posterior compartment syndrome
option_c: Medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS/shin splints)
option_d: Tibialis posterior tendinopathy
rationale: Tibial stress fracture presents with focal pinpoint bony tenderness at a single specific site, positive hop test, and night pain — distinguishing it from MTSS, which has diffuse linear pain over ≥5 cm of the tibial border without a focal point. Night pain and hop test positivity are red flags for fracture. Compartment syndrome is exercise-induced and resolves rapidly with rest.

question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with hip pain localized to the groin, worsened by weight-bearing and internal rotation. FABER and FADIR tests are positive. X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation at the femoral head. Which diagnosis is MOST consistent?
option_a: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (trochanteric bursitis)
option_b: Hip osteoarthritis
option_c: Femoro-acetabular impingement syndrome (FAIS)
option_d: Iliopsoas tendinopathy
rationale: Hip OA presents with groin-predominant pain, progressive limitation particularly in IR and flexion, capsular pattern restriction, and radiographic joint space narrowing with osteophytes. FABER and FADIR positivity in context of radiographic changes confirms OA over FAI (which has similar clinical findings but typically in younger patients without joint space narrowing). Trochanteric bursitis causes lateral hip pain.

question_text: A 38-year-old male construction worker sustains acute right knee injury with a valgus force and foot planted. The valgus stress test is positive at 30° flexion with medial joint line tenderness. X-ray is negative for fracture. Which structure is MOST likely injured?
option_a: Medial collateral ligament (MCL)
option_b: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
option_c: Lateral collateral ligament (LCL)
option_d: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)
rationale: Valgus stress testing at 30° of knee flexion isolates the medial collateral ligament (MCL). A positive test with medial pain and increased laxity indicates MCL sprain. The foot-planted valgus mechanism is the classic MCL injury pattern. LCL is tested with varus stress. ACL injury typically involves a 'pop' and positive Lachman/anterior drawer. PCL is injured by a posterior tibial force with knee flexed.

question_text: A 22-year-old female volleyball player presents with anterior knee pain worsened by prolonged sitting (theatre sign), stair descent, and jumping. Clarke's grind test reproduces pain. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
option_a: Patellar tendinopathy at the inferior pole
option_b: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS)
option_c: Hoffa's fat pad impingement syndrome
option_d: Prepatellar bursitis
rationale: PFPS presents with anterior knee pain worsened by activities that load the patellofemoral joint: prolonged sitting (theatre sign), descending stairs, squatting, and jumping. Clarke's test is characteristic. Patellar tendinopathy causes inferior patellar pole pain worsened by jumping. Fat pad impingement is worse in hyperextension. Prepatellar bursitis causes anterior patellar swelling and is not worsened by sitting.

question_text: A physiotherapist uses the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) to measure outcomes for a patient with chronic low back pain. What is the established MCID for the PSFS individual item score?
option_a: 0.5 points on the 0–10 scale
option_b: 2 points on the individual item 0–10 scale
option_c: 5 points on the 0–10 scale
option_d: No established MCID exists for the PSFS
rationale: The MCID for the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) is 2 points on the individual item 0–10 scale, or 1 point on the average score. This has been validated across multiple musculoskeletal conditions including low back pain, neck pain, and extremity conditions. The PSFS allows patients to identify their own most important functional limitations, making it highly responsive to change.

question_text: A 48-year-old woman is referred for physiotherapy with De Quervain's tenosynovitis. The Finkelstein test is positive. Which tendons are involved in this condition?
option_a: Extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the 3rd extensor compartment
option_b: Flexor pollicis longus in the carpal tunnel
option_c: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis in the 2nd extensor compartment
option_d: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the 1st dorsal extensor compartment
rationale: De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves stenosing tenosynovitis of the 1st dorsal extensor compartment at the radial styloid, containing the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB). The Finkelstein test (thumb in palm, wrist ulnar deviated) stretches and compresses these tendons, reproducing pain at the radial styloid. The 3rd compartment contains EPL; 2nd compartment contains ECRL and ECRB.

question_text: During assessment of a patient with suspected rotator cuff pathology, which physical examination test has the HIGHEST sensitivity for detecting any rotator cuff tear when used for screening?
option_a: Empty can test (Jobe's test)
option_b: Drop arm test
option_c: Lift-off test (Gerber's)
option_d: Painful arc sign (61°–120° of abduction)
rationale: The painful arc sign (pain during the 60°–120° arc of glenohumeral abduction) has the highest sensitivity (~74–98%) of individual tests for detecting rotator cuff pathology and is best used as a screening test. The drop arm test has high specificity but low sensitivity. The empty can is sensitive for supraspinatus. The lift-off test is specific for subscapularis but is not a broad screening tool.

question_text: A physiotherapist applies the Flynn clinical prediction rule to a patient with acute low back pain to determine eligibility for lumbar manipulation. Which combination of findings MOST accurately reflects the 5-factor CPR?
option_a: Symptom duration <16 days, no symptoms below the knee, FABQ Work subscale <19, lumbar hypomobility, and hip IR >35° on at least one side
option_b: Duration <30 days, positive SLR, BMI >25, fear avoidance beliefs >40, and restricted hip extension
option_c: Age <45, positive Kemp's test, pain with extension, no neurological signs, and normal SLR
option_d: Duration <16 days, bilateral hip flexion >90°, positive provocation discography, and lumbar hypermobility
rationale: The Flynn CPR (2002) for lumbar manipulation success includes 5 factors: (1) symptom duration <16 days, (2) no symptoms distal to the knee, (3) FABQ Work subscale <19, (4) lumbar hypomobility, (5) hip IR >35° on one side. Presence of 4 or 5 factors raises post-test probability of success to 95%. This is the most studied CPR in physiotherapy.

question_text: A 65-year-old male with known gout presents with acute swelling, warmth, and erythema of the left first MTP joint. During an acute gout attack, which physiotherapy modality is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Therapeutic ultrasound at 1 MHz, 1.5 W/cm² for 5 minutes to the MTP joint
option_b: Ice application and non-weightbearing rest with protected footwear
option_c: Grade III MTP joint mobilization in flexion and extension
option_d: Iontophoresis with dexamethasone 4 mg/mL to the inflamed joint
rationale: During an acute gout attack, the priority is symptom management: rest, elevation, and ice (cryotherapy) to reduce pain and inflammation. Any mechanical stress (mobilization) or thermal therapy (heat, ultrasound) can worsen the acute inflammatory response. Non-weightbearing or protected weight-bearing protects the joint. Joint mobilization is contraindicated during acute inflammatory arthropathy.

question_text: A patient following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction with a bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) graft at 12 weeks post-surgery complains of anterior knee pain and difficulty kneeling. What is the MOST likely complication specific to BPTB grafts?
option_a: Graft tunnel widening from stress shielding
option_b: Cyclops lesion causing terminal extension loss
option_c: Hamstring muscle weakness and tightness
option_d: Anterior knee pain and patellar tendon harvest site morbidity
rationale: BPTB grafts harvest the central third of the patellar tendon with bone plugs. The most common complication specific to BPTB is anterior knee pain, pain with kneeling, and patellar tendon harvest site morbidity (including patellar stress fracture risk). Hamstring weakness is a complication of hamstring tendon graft. Cyclops lesion can occur with any graft. BPTB is considered the gold standard for strength but carries higher anterior knee morbidity.

question_text: A 68-year-old man presents 6 weeks post-right MCA stroke with left-sided UMN weakness. The Fugl-Meyer Assessment upper extremity score is 22/66. Which Brunnstrom stage does this MOST likely correspond to?
option_a: Stage 3 — full limb synergies performed voluntarily, spasticity at peak
option_b: Stage 2 — beginning of spasticity, minimal synergy
option_c: Stage 1 — flaccidity, no voluntary movement
option_d: Stage 4 — beginning to deviate from synergy with reduced spasticity
rationale: Fugl-Meyer UE scores of 0–22 correspond approximately to Brunnstrom Stages 1–3 (flaccidity through full synergy). A score of 22/66 represents Stage 3, where full limb synergies can be performed voluntarily but movement out of synergy is not yet possible. Stage 4 begins at approximately 23–38 and allows some deviation from synergy patterns.

question_text: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient with incomplete C5 spinal cord injury (AIS C). According to the ASIA Impairment Scale, which definition BEST describes AIS C?
option_a: Motor function preserved below the neurological level; more than half of key muscles below NLI are graded less than 3/5
option_b: Sensory but not motor function is preserved below the neurological level
option_c: No motor or sensory function preserved below the neurological level of injury
option_d: Motor function preserved below the neurological level; at least half of key muscles below NLI are graded 3/5 or greater
rationale: ASIA Impairment Scale: A = complete (no S/M below NLI); B = sensory incomplete (sensory but no motor below NLI); C = motor incomplete (motor preserved but >50% of key muscles below NLI are <3/5); D = motor incomplete (≥50% of key muscles below NLI are ≥3/5); E = normal. AIS C indicates preserved but predominantly non-functional motor strength below the lesion.

question_text: A patient with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis reports severe fatigue that consistently worsens with heat exposure. Which physiological phenomenon explains heat-induced symptom exacerbation in MS?
option_a: Uhthoff's phenomenon — demyelinated axons have further impaired conduction as temperature rises, causing transient conduction block
option_b: Heat causes new inflammatory demyelination at previously unaffected CNS sites
option_c: Increased core temperature triggers autoimmune T-cell activation initiating a new relapse
option_d: Heat-induced vasodilation reduces cerebral perfusion pressure causing symptom worsening
rationale: Uhthoff's phenomenon describes the transient worsening of MS symptoms with increased body temperature. Demyelinated axons have a reduced conduction safety factor; even a small rise in temperature (0.5°C) can block conduction in partially myelinated fibres. This is a conduction block, not a true relapse or new demyelination. Symptoms reverse when temperature normalizes.

question_text: A 75-year-old woman is referred for balance rehabilitation after a fall. The Berg Balance Scale score is 42/56. Which fall risk category does this represent?
option_a: Low fall risk — no intervention required
option_b: Medium fall risk — balance training and monitoring are indicated
option_c: High fall risk — wheelchair mobility is recommended
option_d: Very high fall risk — bed rest is indicated
rationale: Berg Balance Scale: ≥45 = low fall risk; 41–44 = medium fall risk (1.7–3.5× increased fall risk, balance training indicated); ≤40 = high fall risk (nearly 100% fall risk, assistive device may be indicated). A score of 42 falls in the medium risk category, indicating that balance training is warranted with careful monitoring for progression.

question_text: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is in the acute progressive phase. The MOST important physiotherapy safety precaution during this phase is:
option_a: Avoiding passive ROM to prevent heterotopic ossification
option_b: Monitoring for autonomic instability including cardiac arrhythmias and labile blood pressure during all activities
option_c: Encouraging maximal aerobic exercise to prevent deconditioning
option_d: Initiating aggressive respiratory muscle strengthening immediately
rationale: GBS frequently causes autonomic dysfunction (labile BP, cardiac arrhythmias, orthostatic hypotension, sweating abnormalities) that can be life-threatening. During the progressive phase, autonomic monitoring is the paramount safety consideration during any physiotherapy intervention. High-intensity exercise is contraindicated. Respiratory monitoring (VC, MIP) is important but cardiac monitoring takes priority.

question_text: A patient with T10 complete SCI (AIS A) uses a manual wheelchair and complains of bilateral shoulder pain. The MOST common cause and MOST appropriate preventive strategy are:
option_a: Rotator cuff tendinopathy from propulsion; transition to power wheelchair exclusively
option_b: Glenohumeral instability; posterior capsule strengthening program
option_c: Shoulder impingement from propulsion biomechanics; optimize push pattern and strengthen rotator cuff
option_d: AC joint arthritis; prescribe NSAIDs and avoid manual wheelchair use
rationale: Shoulder pain in manual wheelchair users is predominantly caused by rotator cuff impingement and tendinopathy from repetitive overhead loading during propulsion and transfers. Prevention centers on optimizing wheelchair fit and push pattern (semi-circular arc rather than arc-and-snap), strengthening rotator cuff muscles, maintaining shoulder ROM, and reducing peak contact forces. Complete avoidance of manual wheelchair is unnecessary with proper technique.

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive ascending weakness over 3 weeks following a respiratory infection. EMG shows reduced nerve conduction velocities and prolonged distal latencies. Which diagnosis is MOST consistent?
option_a: Myasthenia gravis with fatigable proximal weakness
option_b: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with mixed UMN/LMN signs
option_c: Multiple sclerosis relapse involving the spinal cord
option_d: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy)
rationale: GBS (AIDP) presents with ascending flaccid weakness following infection or vaccination, over days to weeks. EMG/NCS shows a demyelinating pattern: reduced conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, conduction block. CSF shows albuminocytological dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count). Myasthenia gravis shows fatigable proximal weakness; ALS has UMN and LMN signs; MS relapses involve central demyelination.

question_text: A physiotherapist applies NMES to the quadriceps of a patient with femoral nerve injury. Which parameter set MOST effectively produces a strong, fatigue-resistant muscle contraction for strengthening?
option_a: 2 Hz frequency, 50 µs pulse width, continuous mode
option_b: 35–50 Hz frequency, 200–400 µs pulse width, 10 seconds on/50 seconds off
option_c: 100 Hz frequency, 50 µs pulse width, 30 seconds on/10 seconds off
option_d: 150 Hz frequency, 400 µs pulse width, continuous mode
rationale: For NMES targeting skeletal muscle strengthening: 35–50 Hz produces tetanic contraction (sufficient to fuse twitches); 200–400 µs pulse width is needed to depolarize larger motor axons; duty cycle 1:5 (10 seconds on/50 seconds off) prevents excessive fatigue and allows recovery. Very high frequencies (100 Hz+) cause rapid fatigue. Low frequencies (2 Hz) produce twitch contractions insufficient for strengthening.

question_text: A 48-year-old male referred for right facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) 5 days after onset is unable to close his right eye completely. Which House-Brackmann grade does this MOST likely represent?
option_a: Grade IV — moderately severe dysfunction; incomplete eye closure with maximum effort
option_b: Grade III — moderate dysfunction; eye closes with effort but not completely at rest
option_c: Grade II — slight dysfunction with complete eye closure on effort
option_d: Grade V — severe dysfunction; barely perceptible facial movement
rationale: House-Brackmann Grade IV (moderately severe): obvious weakness or disfiguring asymmetry; normal symmetry and tone at rest; forehead: none to slight movement; eye: INCOMPLETE closure even with maximum effort; mouth: asymmetric with effort. Inability to fully close the eye (lagophthalmos) is the hallmark of Grade IV. Grade III still achieves eye closure with effort. Grade V allows only barely perceptible motion.

question_text: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with right hemiplegia post-stroke using constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT). What is the MINIMUM impairment criterion the patient must meet to be a candidate for standard CIMT?
option_a: Fugl-Meyer UE score >50/66
option_b: Ability to pick up a 500 g object from a table with the affected hand
option_c: At least 10° active wrist extension AND 10° active finger extension on the affected side
option_d: Full active extension of all digits of the affected hand
rationale: The inclusion criterion for standard CIMT (Taub protocol) requires ≥10° active wrist extension and ≥10° active extension in at least two digits of the affected hand. This ensures the patient has sufficient motor function to benefit from intensive practice. Patients below this threshold may be candidates for modified CIMT with different task structures. The 500 g lift criterion is not a validated threshold.

question_text: A 3-day post-TBI patient (initial GCS 9, now 13) is referred for physiotherapy in the neuro-ICU. Which tool is the MOST appropriate for measuring post-traumatic amnesia in the acute setting?
option_a: Fugl-Meyer Assessment for sensorimotor impairment
option_b: Modified Rankin Scale for functional outcome
option_c: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
option_d: Westmead Post-Traumatic Amnesia Scale (WPTAS)
rationale: The Westmead PTA Scale (WPTAS) is the gold standard for measuring and monitoring post-traumatic amnesia in the acute TBI setting. It assesses orientation and memory storage (12 items including name, age, date, and 3 picture cards). PTA duration is one of the strongest predictors of TBI severity and long-term outcome. The FIM and Rankin Scale measure functional disability, not PTA.

question_text: A patient with Parkinson's disease demonstrates the pull test (retropulsion test). The patient takes 3 steps backward before recovering balance independently. According to the UPDRS Part III, what score should be assigned?
option_a: 0 — Normal, recovers with 1–2 steps
option_b: 1 — Three or more retropulsive steps but recovers independently
option_c: 2 — Would fall if not caught by the examiner
option_d: 3 — Very unstable, tends to lose balance spontaneously
rationale: UPDRS Part III Item 30 (Postural Stability/Pull Test): 0 = normal (1–2 steps to recover); 1 = 3 or more retropulsive steps, recovers independently; 2 = retropulsion without independent recovery (examiner must catch); 3 = very unstable, loses balance without external perturbation. Three backward steps with independent recovery = Score 1.

question_text: A physiotherapist assesses sensation in a post-stroke patient using Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments. The patient cannot detect the 5.07 (10g) monofilament. This indicates loss of:
option_a: Protective sensation
option_b: Light touch discrimination only
option_c: Two-point discrimination
option_d: Proprioception and deep pressure
rationale: Semmes-Weinstein monofilament 5.07 (10g) is the threshold for protective sensation. Inability to detect this filament means the patient has lost protective sensation and is at risk of injury from undetected pressure or trauma. 3.61 (0.4g) = normal light touch; 4.31 (2g) = diminished light touch; 5.07 (10g) = loss of protective sensation; 6.10 (75g) = deep pressure only.

question_text: A patient with right unilateral vestibular hypofunction undergoes vestibular rehabilitation with gaze stabilization exercises. The PRIMARY mechanism by which these exercises improve function is:
option_a: Restoring hair cell function in the right semicircular canals through repeated stimulation
option_b: Strengthening extraocular muscles to mechanically compensate for the VOR deficit
option_c: Promoting central vestibular compensation through brainstem and cerebellar neuroplasticity
option_d: Desensitizing the vestibular system to reduce abnormal sensitivity to motion
rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation for unilateral hypofunction works through central vestibular compensation — neuroplastic adaptation of the CNS to asymmetric peripheral input. The brainstem and cerebellum rebalance resting firing rates and adapt the gain of remaining vestibular reflexes. VOR × 1 and × 2 gaze stabilization exercises provide the movement-related sensory mismatch signals necessary to drive this adaptation. No peripheral hair cell regeneration occurs in humans.

question_text: A 55-year-old male with COPD (GOLD Stage 3) completes a 6-Minute Walk Test. What is the established MCID for the 6MWT in COPD?
option_a: 10 metres
option_b: 25 metres
option_c: 30 metres
option_d: 54 metres
rationale: The MCID for the 6-Minute Walk Test in COPD is consistently reported as 25–30 metres across multiple validation studies, with 30 metres being the most widely cited threshold. Changes less than 25 metres are not considered clinically meaningful. This threshold is critical for interpreting pulmonary rehabilitation outcomes in clinical practice and research.

question_text: During a graded exercise stress test, a patient's ECG shows horizontal ST-segment depression of 2 mm in leads V4–V6 at 85% of maximum predicted heart rate. The MOST appropriate physiotherapist response is:
option_a: Continue the test; ST depression at near-maximal heart rates is a normal training response
option_b: Reduce exercise intensity to 70% HRmax and continue close monitoring
option_c: Terminate the test immediately and notify the supervising physician
option_d: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin and allow the patient to rest on the treadmill
rationale: Horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥2 mm is an absolute indication to terminate an exercise test, representing significant myocardial ischaemia. ACSM guidelines list ≥2 mm ST depression as an absolute test termination criterion. The physician must be immediately notified. Physiotherapists do not administer nitroglycerin; continuing or reducing intensity is inappropriate with active ischaemic ECG changes.

question_text: A patient with COPD has chronic hypercapnia (PaCO2 58 mmHg). The physiological mechanism by which these patients lose their normal CO2-driven respiratory drive is BEST explained by:
option_a: The medullary respiratory centre is destroyed by chronic CO2 accumulation
option_b: Chronic metabolic alkalosis suppresses brainstem breathing centres
option_c: Peripheral chemoreceptors are downregulated by chronic hypoxia
option_d: Renal bicarbonate retention normalizes CSF pH, blunting central chemoreceptor response to CO2
rationale: In chronic hypercapnia, the kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate, which diffuses into the CSF and normalizes CSF pH despite elevated PaCO2. This blunts the central chemoreceptor CO2 response. Consequently, these patients become dependent on hypoxic drive via peripheral chemoreceptors. This is why high-flow oxygen can precipitate hypercapnic respiratory failure in some COPD patients.

question_text: Which spirometric finding pattern is MOST consistent with a diagnosis of bronchial asthma?
option_a: FEV1/FVC >0.70, reduced TLC, increased RV — restrictive pattern
option_b: FEV1/FVC <0.70, no reversibility after bronchodilator, DLCO significantly reduced
option_c: FEV1/FVC >0.70, reduced FVC with normal FEV1 — restrictive pattern
option_d: FEV1/FVC <0.70, reversible after bronchodilator (≥12% and ≥200 mL improvement in FEV1)
rationale: Asthma is characterized by reversible airflow obstruction: FEV1/FVC <0.70 (obstructive pattern) with ≥12% and ≥200 mL improvement in FEV1 post-bronchodilator. COPD shows obstruction without significant reversibility and may have reduced DLCO. Restrictive patterns (normal ratio, reduced FVC or TLC) do not characterize asthma.

question_text: A patient with bronchiectasis produces copious mucopurulent sputum daily. The MOST evidence-based airway clearance technique for independent daily self-management is:
option_a: Postural drainage with percussion requiring a trained caregiver
option_b: Assisted cough with abdominal thrust from a caregiver
option_c: Oscillating positive expiratory pressure (OPEP) device such as the Aerobika or Flutter valve
option_d: Continuous high-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) vest therapy
rationale: Oscillating positive expiratory pressure devices (Flutter, Aerobika, Acapella) are the most widely recommended independent ACT for bronchiectasis. They combine PEP (stenting airways open) with oscillation (mobilizing secretions). Evidence demonstrates good sputum clearance, patient independence, and adherence compared to caregiver-dependent techniques. Active cycle of breathing technique (ACBT) also has strong evidence for self-management.

question_text: Interpreting an arterial blood gas result: pH 7.28, PaCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L. The MOST accurate interpretation is:
option_a: Respiratory alkalosis — hyperventilation causing CO2 to fall
option_b: Metabolic acidosis — primary bicarbonate deficit
option_c: Compensated respiratory acidosis — metabolic alkalosis partially correcting pH
option_d: Uncompensated acute respiratory acidosis — elevated CO2 with normal bicarbonate
rationale: Systematic ABG interpretation: pH 7.28 = acidosis. PaCO2 55 mmHg = elevated (respiratory cause). HCO3- 26 = normal (22–26 mEq/L; no metabolic compensation). Conclusion: acute uncompensated respiratory acidosis. If chronic/compensated, HCO3- would be elevated (>29 mEq/L). The normal bicarbonate confirms this is an acute process without renal compensation.

question_text: A patient with PAD and intermittent claudication participates in supervised exercise. What is the MOST evidence-based exercise intervention for improving claudication walking distance?
option_a: Aquatic therapy at 80% HRmax to avoid pain
option_b: Non-weightbearing cycling to circumvent ischaemic pain entirely
option_c: Supervised treadmill walking to near-maximal claudication pain, with rest intervals, 3 times/week
option_d: Ankle strengthening and flexibility program only
rationale: Supervised treadmill exercise to near-maximal claudication pain (Borg claudication scale 3–4/4) with rest intervals is the gold standard for PAD management. Walking until near-maximal pain, resting, then repeating maximizes collateral vessel development and metabolic adaptation. Meta-analyses demonstrate significant improvements in pain-free and maximal walking distance. Non-weightbearing exercise has significantly less evidence.

question_text: A physiotherapist is designing a pulmonary rehabilitation program for a GOLD Stage 3 COPD patient. What is the MINIMUM recommended duration of supervised outpatient PR to achieve clinically significant benefits?
option_a: 2 weeks of daily intensive sessions
option_b: 4 weeks (12 sessions) of supervised training
option_c: 8 weeks (20 or more sessions) of supervised training
option_d: 6 months of maintenance phase training
rationale: Current GOLD guidelines and ATS/ERS consensus statements recommend a minimum of 8 weeks (≥20 sessions) of supervised pulmonary rehabilitation to achieve clinically significant improvements in exercise capacity, dyspnea, and quality of life in COPD. Programs shorter than 8 weeks show attenuated benefits. 12–16 weeks produces greater and more sustained gains.

question_text: A physiotherapist notes bilateral basilar lung crackles in a patient with left ventricular failure. These crackles do NOT clear with coughing. The MOST appropriate interpretation is:
option_a: Bronchiectasis with retained mucopurulent secretions in the basilar segments
option_b: Pulmonary fibrosis causing late inspiratory crackles bilaterally
option_c: Transudative alveolar fluid causing late inspiratory crackles that do not clear with cough
option_d: Mucus plugging of central airways causing coarse early inspiratory crackles
rationale: Left ventricular failure causes increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure leading to transudation of fluid into the alveoli (pulmonary oedema). This fluid causes fine late-inspiratory crackles at the lung bases that do NOT clear with coughing (unlike secretions). They result from sudden opening of fluid-filled small airways during end-inspiration. Distinguishing from secretion-related crackles guides appropriate physiotherapy intervention.

question_text: A physiotherapist prescribes exercise for a patient taking metoprolol (beta-1 selective blocker) for hypertension. Which exercise prescription modification is MOST important?
option_a: Use measured peak HR from a graded exercise test (on current medication) rather than age-predicted HRmax for intensity prescription
option_b: Reduce exercise frequency to once per week to avoid cardiovascular stress
option_c: Use blood pressure as the only exercise intensity guide, ignoring heart rate entirely
option_d: Avoid all aerobic exercise; prescribe resistance training only
rationale: Beta-blockers attenuate the chronotropic response to exercise, making age-predicted HRmax (220 − age) unreliable. The HRmax with beta-blockade is significantly lower than predicted. If using heart rate as an intensity guide, HRmax must be measured via GXT on the current medication dose. Alternatively, RPE (Borg scale 12–14) is used as the primary intensity guide. Using 220-age would result in training at a physiologically inappropriate intensity.

question_text: A physiotherapist in the cardiac ICU notes post-CABG chest tube drainage output of 350 mL/hour over the past 2 hours. The MOST appropriate action is:
option_a: Continue routine physiotherapy mobilization as planned; some drainage is expected
option_b: Increase fluid intake and encourage deep breathing exercises to improve cardiac output
option_c: Document the finding and reassess drainage in 4 hours
option_d: Immediately notify the nursing staff and physician — excessive drainage may indicate haemorrhage
rationale: Post-cardiac surgery chest tube output >200 mL/hour for 2+ consecutive hours is a critical warning sign of excessive bleeding requiring immediate medical escalation. This is a potential emergency requiring immediate notification of the surgical team. Physiotherapy mobilization should be suspended. Normal post-operative drainage is <100 mL/hour and decreasing. Physiotherapists must recognize and escalate this finding.

question_text: A 78-year-old nursing home resident has developed a pressure injury over the right ischial tuberosity. Using NPUAP/EPUAP classification, Stage 2 is defined as:
option_a: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin
option_b: Partial thickness skin loss with exposed dermis presenting as a shallow open ulcer or intact/ruptured blister
option_c: Full thickness tissue loss with visible subcutaneous fat but no bone, tendon, or muscle visible
option_d: Full thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle
rationale: NPUAP/EPUAP Pressure Injury Staging: Stage 1 = non-blanchable erythema of intact skin; Stage 2 = partial thickness skin loss with exposed dermis — shallow open ulcer or intact/ruptured blister; Stage 3 = full thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible; Stage 4 = full thickness tissue loss with exposed bone/tendon/muscle; Unstageable = slough/eschar obscures depth.

question_text: Which THREE parameters does the PUSH (Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing) tool measure to track pressure injury healing over time?
option_a: Wound surface area, exudate amount, and tissue type
option_b: Wound depth, periwound temperature, and odour
option_c: Wound colour, patient pain level, and exudate type
option_d: Tunnel length, wound surface area, and surrounding skin integrity
rationale: The PUSH tool measures three parameters: (1) wound surface area (length × width), (2) exudate amount (none/light/moderate/heavy), and (3) tissue type (closed/epithelial/granulation/slough/necrotic). Each is scored and summed for a total score of 0–17; decreasing score indicates healing. It is validated specifically for monitoring pressure injury healing.

question_text: A physiotherapist applies pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy near a chronic wound. Which precaution is MOST important to screen for before application?
option_a: Patient allergy to adhesive dressings or latex
option_b: Presence of implanted electronic devices such as pacemakers or deep brain stimulators
option_c: Patient's serum albumin and pre-albumin levels
option_d: Wound bacterial culture and antibiotic sensitivity results
rationale: PEMF generates oscillating electromagnetic fields that can interfere with implanted electronic devices (pacemakers, ICDs, cochlear implants, deep brain stimulators). This is the primary safety contraindication. Implanted device malfunction can be immediately life-threatening. All other considerations, while clinically relevant, are not safety-critical contraindications for the modality itself.

question_text: A wound has 70% yellow slough and 30% granulation tissue. Which debridement method is MOST selective, removing only non-viable tissue while leaving healthy granulation intact?
option_a: Sharp surgical debridement with a scalpel
option_b: Wet-to-dry mechanical debridement with gauze
option_c: Enzymatic debridement with collagenase
option_d: High-pressure irrigation at >15 psi
rationale: Enzymatic debridement (collagenase, papain-urea) is selective: it chemically digests necrotic tissue proteins while leaving viable tissue intact. Sharp debridement is the fastest but non-selective and requires trained practitioners. Wet-to-dry dressings are non-selective and damage granulation tissue. High-pressure irrigation (>15 psi) can drive bacteria into tissues and damage granulation beds.

question_text: In burn rehabilitation, which intervention is MOST important during the acute phase to prevent scar contracture of the anterior neck?
option_a: Cervical collar fabricated in neutral flexion to protect the wound bed from tension
option_b: Cervical traction applied for 20 minutes twice daily to distract the healing tissue
option_c: Active ROM within pain-free range, avoiding cervical extension at all times
option_d: Custom thermoplastic collar maintaining cervical extension to counteract contractile forces
rationale: Anterior neck burns have a strong propensity for scar contracture in cervical flexion (chin-to-chest deformity). The standard intervention is fabrication of a conforming thermoplastic collar or custom cervical orthosis maintaining the neck in extension and neutral rotation, worn during sleep and rest. This counteracts the contractile forces of healing burn scar. Active ROM into extension is also prescribed during waking hours.
